item.title: How to back up photos to a USB drive without uploading them
item.description: Your photos don't need a cloud to be safe. A USB drive plugged into your phone holds the whole backup — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

item.title: USB photo backup on Android: back up photos to an external drive without uploading them
item.description: Your phone's camera roll fits on a drive you can hold. A USB photo backup keeps the whole copy in your pocket — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

item.title: How to back up DCIM to OTG storage on Android
item.description: DCIM is where your Android phone keeps its camera photos — and OTG is how a USB drive plugs straight into that phone. Put the two together and your whole camera roll copies to a drive you can hold, with no computer and no upload in between.

item.title: How to copy photos to a USB stick on Android
item.description: A USB stick is the simplest photo backup there is: no account, no upload, no monthly fee — just your photos on a drive you can hold. And on Android you don't need a computer in between: the stick plugs straight into the phone.

item.title: How to back up photos offline on Android — no cloud, no account
item.description: Most "backup" apps start by uploading your photos to someone else's server. An offline backup never does: your photos copy from your phone straight to a drive you can hold, with no account, no upload, and nothing to log into.

item.title: How to back up photos to an external drive on Android
item.description: An external drive is the simplest photo backup there is: a drive you can hold, with your photos on it, and no cloud in between. On Android the drive plugs straight into the phone — no computer needed.

item.title: How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive
item.description: Your phone is full because your photos are. Move them to a USB drive you can hold, check the copy, then delete the originals — and the storage warning goes away without losing a single picture.

item.title: SnapDisk vs VaultDrive: USB photo backup on Android, compared
item.description: Two Android apps that copy your photos to a USB drive — no cloud, no account, no upload. Here is how they actually differ, from the facts we could verify as of November 2026.

item.title: Back up WhatsApp photos to a USB drive on Android (no computer)
item.description: Your WhatsApp photos are files on your phone — in a folder you can point a backup app at. Plug a USB drive into the phone and copy them straight to it, no computer, no upload.

item.title: Transfer photos from Android to a USB drive automatically (no manual copy)
item.description: Moving photos to a USB drive by hand means opening a file manager, picking files one by one, and hoping nothing gets missed. Plug the drive in, tap once, and let the whole library copy itself.

item.title: Back up Samsung Galaxy photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Galaxy phones are the most common Android phones there are, and Samsung gives you two ways to get photos onto a USB drive — but neither one is a photo backup that runs itself. Here is what Samsung offers, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Google Pixel photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Pixel phones have no SD-card slot and no Samsung-style file manager — but a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up OnePlus photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: OnePlus phones hide one extra switch before a USB drive works at all — OxygenOS turns OTG off unless you enable it. Once it's on, a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is My Files. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Xiaomi photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Xiaomi phones hide one extra switch before a USB drive works at all — on many MIUI and HyperOS phones OTG is off unless you enable it, and it switches itself off after about 10 minutes. Once it's on, a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Mi File Manager. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Motorola photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Motorola phones run near-stock Android, so there is no OTG switch to hunt for — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up videos from Android to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Videos are the files that fill a phone first — and the ones the manual copy handles worst, one long file at a time. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Huawei photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Huawei phones have their own built-in backup app, but it writes an encrypted archive — not plain photos you can open anywhere. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is the Files app. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Sony Xperia photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Sony's Xperia phones run near-stock Android with almost no Sony apps on board — Google Photos is the gallery, Files by Google is the file manager — and Sony's own backup tool needs a PC. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up LG photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: LG stopped making phones in 2021, so no LG guide or LG tool will ever be written for this — and LG's own backup tools move data phone-to-phone or phone-to-PC, never phone-to-USB as plain photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Oppo photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Realme photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Vivo photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Honor photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Nokia photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Asus photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Infinix photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Tecno photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Nothing Phone photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Nothing phones (Phone (1), Phone (2), Phone (2a), and the CMF Phone 1) run Nothing OS — a near-stock Android skin — with OTG support on the main Phone models: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Phone (1), Phone (2), Phone (2a), and Phone (2a) Plus, and Nothing's own support site documents OTG as a feature — but the CMF Phone 1 is the exception to check, because spec tables disagree on whether it supports OTG at all. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any Nothing phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any POCO phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

And iQOO's own backup tools are iQOO Cloud (vivo Cloud) and Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools, which back your photos up to the cloud or to a computer, not to a USB drive as plain files. And HTC has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its own tool is HTC Sync Manager, a desktop app that backs your pictures up to a PC — and it is discontinued, support ended — and the other routes are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current HTC. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Blackview photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Blackview. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.description: Sonim's Android phones (XP8 and XP10) have USB host support on at least the XP8 — the XP8 user guide lists the USB-C port as "High Speed, OTG" — and Sonim has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: Sonim SCOUT is a device-management app, not a backup, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. One honest caveat up front: the XP10 datasheet I found does not list OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it, and the XP5s is not an Android phone at all — it runs a proprietary OS, so SnapDisk cannot install on it. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Kyocera photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Kyocera's DuraForce Android phones (Pro 2, Ultra 5G, PRO 3, and DuraSport) have USB host support on at least two of them — the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the DuraForce Pro 2, and the DuraSport's spec pages list its port as "USB Type-C, USB On-The-Go" — and Kyocera has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Hammer 6 LTE is a feature phone, not an Android phone at all, so SnapDisk cannot install on it, and the original Hammer Iron runs Android 4.2 and the AXE M LTE runs Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up FOSSiBOT photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: FOSSiBOT's rugged F-series Android phones (F101, F101 Pro, F102, F107 Pro, F110 Pro 5G, F112 Pro, and F113) list USB OTG support in their spec tables, and FOSSiBOT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up UMIDIGI Bison photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Handheld photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The refreshed Nautiz X2, the Nautiz X6, the Nautiz X9, the Nautiz X41 and the Nautiz X81 are Handheld Group's Nautiz line of rugged enterprise Android handhelds (refreshed X2; X6; X9; X41; X81), and Handheld has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no Handheld-specific file advice pointing at a USB drive turned up at all. item.title: Back up i.safe MOBILE photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The IS530.1, the IS530.2, the IS530.RG, the IS530.M1, the IS540.1, the IS540.2 and the IS655 are i.safe MOBILE's intrinsically safe Android smartphones (IS530.1; IS530.2; IS530.RG; IS530.M1; IS540.1; IS540.2; IS655), and i.safe MOBILE has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its manuals point at Google's Android support pages for operating-system questions, not at any i.safe backup app. Five honest caveats up front: no source found labels any i.safe MOBILE USB port OTG — every datasheet and manual says only that the USB interface is for charging and data transfer — so plug in a drive and look for the mount notification, or run a USB OTG Checker app, before buying an adapter; i.safe's own manuals say to use the USB interface only outside explosion-hazardous areas — wired USB connections are prohibited inside them, and only approved accessories may be connected to it — so do the backup outside the hazardous area, with the i.safe PROTECTOR 2.0 cable the device shipped with; the Android version differs by source on two models — the IS540.1 runs Android 12 at launch in one benchmark listing and Android 14 in a reseller listing, and the IS530.2 runs Android 13 in its 2024 datasheet but Android 10, upgradable to 13, in an older reseller sheet — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; the IS655 is the only covered model with micro-USB instead of USB-C, so it needs a micro-USB OTG adapter, and its battery is integrated, not replaceable; and Google Play comes with the EEA versions only — the manuals say the EEA version comes with the Google app and Google Play, and some variants, such as the mining versions, may not have them — so check for the Play Store on your unit, and sideload the APK if it is absent. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Ecom Smart-Ex photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Seventeen honest caveats up front: the one-tap route exists on six phones only — the Canvas 1, Canvas Infinity, IN 1, IN 1b, IN Note 1 and IN 2b all clear Android 7.0 and list USB OTG — so only those six get the automated backup; one phone lists OTG No — the Canvas 2 (2017), per gadgets360 and hardreset99 — so on that one there is no phone route at all, even though it clears Android 7.0 and can install SnapDisk; one phone's OTG is disputed — the Canvas 2 2018, where bmobile's listing says Micro USB 2.0 with O-T-G function support while findpare says USB OTG No — so on that one the drive mounting is the test before counting on the one-tap route; one phone clears Android 7.0 but no source found states OTG for it — the Canvas 2 Plus (2018), where gadgets360 leaves the OTG line blank and smartprix lists only USB charging — so on that one the drive mounting is the test too, and SnapDisk installs on it but the one-tap route is unproven until a drive mounts; no covered Micromax phone is below the Android 7.0 minimum at all — the oldest, the Canvas 1, Canvas 2 (2017), Canvas 2 2018 and Canvas 2 Plus (2018), run Android 7.0 exactly — so unlike most brands in this series there is no Micromax phone here that cannot run SnapDisk; the connector splits the range in two — the IN 1, IN 1b, IN Note 1 and IN 2b take USB-C, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into those four, while the Canvas 1, Canvas Infinity, Canvas 2 (2017), Canvas 2 2018 and Canvas 2 Plus (2018) take micro-USB 2.0 and need a micro-USB OTG adapter — and a USB-C adapter does not fit a micro-USB port, so check your unit's port before buying anything; the Canvas 1's microSD ceiling is two numbers — up to 32 GB per gadgets360, indianexpress and gadgetsnow, up to 64 GB per gadgetguide4u and phoneradar; one spec site lists a second Canvas 1 entirely — phonepik's Canvas1 page says released 15 June 2023 on Android 14 with a 6.67-inch display, against the July 2017 launch, 5-inch display and Android 7.0 every other source lists — so the 2023 listing is not used as a source here; the Canvas Infinity's Android version is three numbers — Android 7.0 at launch per gadgets360's launch report, Android 7.1.2 per smartprix, Android 7.1 upgradeable to 8.0 per mobilegizmo — and its battery is two numbers — 2900 mAh per gadgets360, 2980 mAh per smartprix, phonesdata and phonemore — either way it clears 7.0; the same site lists a second Canvas Infinity too — phonepik's page says released 15 June 2023 with a 6.67-inch display and an 8 MP ultrawide second camera, against the August 2017 launch, 5.7-inch display and single 13 MP rear camera every other source lists — so that listing is not used as a source here either; the Canvas 2 2018's Android version is two numbers — Android 7.0 per smartprix, Android 7.1 per bmobile — either way it clears 7.0; the IN Note 1's microSD ceiling is two numbers — up to 256 GB in a dedicated slot per mysmartprice, cashify and hindustantimes, up to 1 TB per techtoreview's summary — and the same techtoreview page lists its card slot as No in one table and its OS as Android 10 with FunTouch 10.5, which is Vivo's interface, not Micromax's — so that page is not used as a source for the IN Note 1 here; the IN Note 1's front camera is two numbers — 16 MP per phonebunch, 5 MP per ubergizmo; one spec site lists a second IN 2b too — phonepik's 6 GB RAM page says Android 14 with a June 2023 launch, against Android 11 with an August 2021 launch per smartprix, gadgets360, cashify and phonepik's own other page — so the Android 14 listing is not used as a source here; VaultDrive needs Android 8 or later per its own site, so the five Canvas models on Android 7.0 or 7.1 cannot run it either — and AppBrain lists 12.1 or later, which no covered Micromax phone clears, since the newest covered models run Android 11; no source found names the stock file manager on a Micromax phone, so Method 2 uses Files by Google or the built-in file manager, whatever it is called on your unit; and the search results for this query are a YouTube video, a Play app listing, a forum thread and three generic Android guides — not one of them is a Micromax-specific guide at all. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.description: Karbonn Mobiles is an Indian budget phone maker, and the covered models are the Titanium line — the Titanium Jumbo (2017), Titanium Jumbo 2 (2018), Titanium Frames S7 (2018) and Titanium S9 Plus (2020) on the new end, and the Titanium S5 (2013), S5 Plus (2013), S5i (2014), S7 (2013), S9 (2013), Titanium X (2013), Hexa, Octane Plus, Mach One S310 (2015) and Mach Two S360 (2015) on the old end (Jumbo; Jumbo 2; Frames S7; S9 Plus; S5; S5 Plus; S5i; S7; S9; Titanium X; Hexa; Octane Plus; Mach One; Mach Two), and Karbonn has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no Karbonn-specific backup advice turned up in any source beyond a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos. every covered model takes micro-USB — all fourteen, with no USB-C model in this guide — so a regular USB drive needs a micro-USB OTG adapter on every one of the four, and a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into none of them; one phone takes no microSD card at all — the Hexa, per phonebunch — so the card-reader route in Method 4 does not exist on it, and it is the only covered model with no local copy route besides the computer; one phone's OTG is disputed — the S9, where phonebunch lists USB On-the-go and OTG Supported while gadgets360 says USB OTG No — though the dispute changes nothing for the backup, since the S9 runs Android 4.2 and cannot run SnapDisk either way; the S9 Plus launch is two dates — 20 January 2020 per one gadgetsnow comparison, 22 October 2020 per another gadgetsnow comparison — either way it runs Android 9.0; the Mach One's internal storage is two numbers — 8 GB per gadgets360, 16 GB per the Economic Times review; the Mach Two's Android is 4.4.2 with a Lollipop upgrade promised — pkgsm lists it as upgradable to 5.0 — but even 5.0 is below SnapDisk's 7.0 minimum, so the upgrade changes nothing about the backup; one spec site lists a second Jumbo and a second S9 Plus entirely — phonepik's pages say both were released 15 June 2023 on Android 14 with a 6.67-inch display, against the October 2017 Jumbo launch on Android 7.0 with a 5-inch display and the 2020 S9 Plus launch on Android 9.0 that every other source lists — so neither 2023 listing is used as a source here; FotoSafe needs Android 9 or later with USB host or OTG support, so only the S9 Plus clears it; no source found names the stock file manager on a Karbonn phone, so Method 2 uses Files by Google or the built-in file manager, whatever it is called on your unit; all four clear Android 7.0 — the lowest runs Android 8.0 — so there is no below-7.0 phone in this article and no phone that cannot install SnapDisk; the install route splits on the OS: ShiftOS-G ships with Google services and the Play Store, so SnapDisk installs from Play once the listing is live and from the GitHub APK until then, while ShiftOS-L ships without Google services, so SnapDisk installs from the GitHub APK only — and on a phone running Ubuntu Touch instead of ShiftOS there is no SnapDisk route at all, while on /e/OS the GitHub APK installs because /e/OS runs Android apps; all four take USB Type-C, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them and there is no micro-USB adapter question anywhere in this article; all four take a microSD card — so the card-reader route in Method 4 is proven on all four — with the ceilings split: the SHIFT5me takes a card up to 256 GB and the SHIFT6mq up to 512 GB, no source states a ceiling for the SHIFT6m at all, and the SHIFTphone 8's ceiling is two numbers — up to 256 GB per the /e/OS device page, up to 2 TB per Murena; the SHIFTphone 8's second camera is two numbers — a 50 MP ultra-wide-angle camera per SHIFT's own page, 32 MP per UL benchmarks; the SHIFTphone 8's battery is two numbers — 3850 mAh per UL benchmarks, 3820 mAh per Murena, the /e/OS device page and Stuff; the SHIFTphone 8's chip is two listings — the QCM6490 per UL benchmarks and the /e/OS device page, the Snapdragon 778G per Murena; the SHIFT6mq's thickness is two numbers — 9.7 mm per UL benchmarks, 8.5 mm per the Ubuntu Touch device page; the SHIFTphone 8's release is two dates — 2024 per the /e/OS device page, end of May / beginning of June 2025 expected per Wikipedia's table, which predates the launch; the SHIFTphone 8's Android version is the base, not necessarily what is on the phone today — UL benchmarks lists Android 14, SHIFT promises Android upgrades through 2036 and gives an Android 15-to-16 upgrade as the example, and the Murena variant runs /e/OS on AOSP 16 — so an 8 today may run 14, 15 or 16; the SHIFT6mq under postmarketOS lists USB-OTG as not working — but that is postmarketOS, not ShiftOS, so it does not settle the ShiftOS question; VaultDrive needs Android 8 or later per its own site, so all four clear the version floor — the lowest runs Android 8.0 exactly — but the drive-hosting condition is proven on two of the four — so VaultDrive is proven on two of the four — and AppBrain lists 12.1 or later, which only the SHIFTphone 8 clears on Android 14 — so under that stricter listing VaultDrive is proven on one of the four; FotoSafe needs Android 9 or later with USB host or OTG support, so the SHIFT5me and the SHIFT6m run Android 8.0 and sit below the version floor entirely — the SHIFT6mq clears the version floor on Android 10 but its OTG is unproven — so FotoSafe is proven on one of the four, the SHIFTphone 8 alone; no source found names the file manager on a Shiftphone, so Method 2 names it only as your file manager app; and the search results for this query are five results — a Dr.Fone guide, a VaultDrive page, a WITNESS blog post, a softhandtech guide and a thegadgetians guide — not one of them is a Shiftphone-specific phone-to-USB photo-backup guide at all. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up LeEco photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: LeEco — short for LeEcosystem, the phone arm of Chinese video-streaming company LeTV — sold eleven phone models between 2015 and 2017, from the Le 1 to the Le Pro 3 Elite, and then the company collapsed: the phones stopped getting updates, and LeEco's own cloud storage shut down in June 2017. The covered models are the Le 1 (2015), Le 1 Pro (2015), Le Max (2015), Le Max Pro (2016), Le 2 (2016), Le 2 Pro (2016), Le Max 2 (2016), Le S3 (2016), Le Pro 3 (2016), Le Pro 3 AI Edition (2017) and Le Pro 3 Elite (2017) (Le 1; Le 1 Pro; Le Max; Le Max Pro; Le 2; Le 2 Pro; Le Max 2; Le S3; Le Pro 3; Le Pro 3 AI Edition; Le Pro 3 Elite), and LeEco has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no LeEco-specific backup advice turned up in any source beyond a computer copy, its own cloud — which ended in June 2017 — or Google Photos on the models that shipped with Google services. Nineteen honest caveats up front: no stock LeEco phone clears Android 7.0 — the highest runs Android 6.0.1 — so SnapDisk does not install on any of the eleven on stock firmware, and there is no below-7.0 exception anywhere in this article; the Android 7.1 update was tested for five models — the Le 2, Le 2 Pro, Le Pro 3, Le Max 2 and Le S3 — as EUI 6.0.28 but never shipped, and the Le Pro 3 and the Le S3 stayed on Android 6.0.1; the custom-ROM exception is documented for one model only — the Le Pro 3, which runs Android 7.1.1 under LineageOS 14.1; USB OTG is Yes on six of the eleven — the Le Max, Le 2, Le 2 Pro, Le Max 2, Le Pro 3 and Le Pro 3 Elite — No on three — the Le 1 Pro, Le Max Pro and Le S3 — and contested on two — the Le 1 and the Le Pro 3 AI Edition; the Le Max 2's OTG is Yes per Gadgets360 and Smartprix, while GSMArena's USB row lists only USB Type-C 2.0 with no OTG; the Le 1's OTG is No per Gadgets360 and FindPare, Yes per UMA Technology; the Le Pro 3 AI Edition's OTG is No per techwikies, while Trak.in lists On-The-Go under its USB connectivity; a microSD card fits one of the eleven — the Le Pro 3 AI Edition, with no ceiling stated — while eight take no card at all, the Le Max Pro's card is contested, and no source states one for the Le S3 or the Le Pro 3 Elite; the Le Max Pro's card is two sources apart — Gadgets360 says no expandable storage, MobileGizmo lists a microSD slot up to 64 GB on the second SIM slot; the Le Max Pro's storage is two numbers — 32 GB per Gadgets360, 64 GB per MobileGizmo; the Le Max's battery is two numbers — 3400 mAh or 3500 mAh per the launch report; the Le 2's chip is two listings — the Helio X20 per some sources, the Snapdragon 652 per others; the Le 2 Pro's chip is two listings — the Helio X20 per Gadgets360, the Helio X25 per phonesdata; VaultDrive needs Android 8 or later per its own site, so none of the eleven clear the version floor — and AppBrain lists 12.1 or later, which none of them clears either — so VaultDrive is proven on none of the eleven; FotoSafe needs Android 9 or later with USB host or OTG support, so none of the eleven clear the version floor either — so FotoSafe is proven on none of the eleven; LeEco's own cloud backup is gone — LeCloud's personal cloud storage ended in June 2017; the China-market Le 1 ships without Google Mobile services, so Google Photos may not be on your unit at all — check for the Photos app before counting on the cloud route; all eleven take USB Type-C, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them and there is no micro-USB adapter question anywhere in this article; and the search results for this query are five results — a softhandtech guide, an EyeFi forum thread, a Dr.Fone guide, a YouTube OTG video and a MobileTrans guide — not one of them is a LeEco-specific phone-to-USB photo-backup guide at all. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Nubia photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Nubia began as ZTE's premium phone brand — the Z5 launched in December 2012 as ZTE's first flagship under the Nubia name — and the Z line has run from that first 5-inch phone to today's Z60 Ultra, with a camera-first reputation and a gaming offshoot, RedMagic, along the way. The covered models are the eleven flagships: the Z5 (2012), Z7 (2014), Z9 (2015), Z11 (2016), Z17 (2017), Z18 (2018), Z20 (2019), Z30 Pro (2021), Z40 Pro (2022), Z50 (2022) and Z60 Ultra (2023) (Z5; Z7; Z9; Z11; Z17; Z18; Z20; Z30 Pro; Z40 Pro; Z50; Z60 Ultra). The mini variants — the Z11 mini, Z11 mini S, Z17 mini and Z18 mini — are not covered here. Nubia has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no Nubia-specific backup advice turned up in any source beyond a computer copy or Google Photos on the models that shipped with Google services. Nineteen honest caveats up front: seven of the eleven clear Android 7.0 — the Z17 on 7.1.1, the Z18 on 8.1, the Z20 on 9.0, the Z30 Pro on 11, the Z40 Pro on 12, the Z50 on 13 and the Z60 Ultra on 14 — so SnapDisk installs on those seven, and four do not — the Z5 on 4.1.1, the Z7 on 4.4.2, the Z9 on 5.0.2 and the Z11 on 6.0 or 6.0.1; the one-tap route is proven on five of the eleven — the Z18, Z20, Z30 Pro, Z40 Pro and Z60 Ultra clear the floor and list USB OTG Yes — while the Z17 and the Z50 clear the floor but their OTG is contested, so on those two the drive mounting is the test; the Z17's OTG is No per Gadgets360, Yes per phonesdata, Smartprix and MobileGizmo; the Z50's OTG is Yes per GSMArena, Kimovil and Smartprix, while phonebunch lists it as Not Supported; the Z5's OTG is unstated in every source found — GSMArena's USB row lists only microUSB 2.0, with no OTG either way; the Z9's Android version is two numbers — 5.2 per GSMArena, 5.0.2 per Smartprix and phonebunch; the Z9's microSD card is contested — GSMArena and Kimovil say No, while Smartprix says Memory Card Supported with a dedicated slot; the Z7's microSD card is contested — PhoneMore says Not supported, while PhoneArena says you can add more via a microSD card; the Z11's microSD ceiling is three numbers — up to 200 GB per MobileGizmo, Smartprix and 91mobiles, up to 256 GB per aivanet, up to 512 GB per GSMArena and phonesdata; the Z11's Android version is two numbers — 6.0 or 6.0.1 per most sources, 6.1 per phonesdata; the Z17's microSD card is contested — Gadgets360 and Smartprix say No, while MobileGizmo lists a microSD slot up to 128 GB on the SIM 2 slot; the Z18's battery is two numbers — 3350 mAh per Smartprix, 3450 mAh per Gadgets360, phonebunch, phonesdata and MobileGizmo; the Z30 Pro's battery is two numbers — 4200 mAh per versus, 4600 mAh per phonebunch; the Z30 Pro's storage is two listings — 256 GB or 512 GB per versus, while phonebunch lists 128 GB as well; the Z5's battery is two numbers — 2300 mAh per GSMArena and techulator, 3000 mAh per Legit Reviews; VaultDrive needs Android 8 or later per its own site, so six of the eleven clear the version floor — and AppBrain lists 12.1 or later, which two clear — the Z50 on Android 13 and the Z60 Ultra on Android 14 — so under that stricter listing VaultDrive is proven on two of the eleven; FotoSafe needs Android 9 or later with USB host or OTG support, so five of the eleven clear the version floor — but the Z50's OTG is contested — so FotoSafe is proven on four of the eleven; a microSD card fits one of the eleven for certain — the Z11, with a contested ceiling — while seven take no card at all, and the card is contested on three — the Z7, the Z9 and the Z17 — so the card-reader route is proven on one model only; and the ports split by age — the Z5, Z7 and Z9 take micro-USB, so those three need a micro-USB OTG adapter, while the Z11 onward take USB Type-C — and the search results for this query are five results — a groovypost guide, an unanswered.io guide, a sekin.in guide, an EyeFi forum thread and a YouTube OTG video — not one of them is a Nubia-specific phone-to-USB photo-backup guide at all. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.
